fields.h1: What Is Sanctification? How God Makes Us Holy
fields.meta_title: What Is Sanctification? How God Makes Us Holy
fields.description: Sanctification is the lifelong work by which God makes a saved person holy. Here is what it is, who does the work, and how to cooperate with it.
fields.body_html:
Most Christians know the moment they were forgiven mattered. Fewer know what to make of everything that comes after — the long, uneven road on which a saved person is slowly made good. That road has a name: sanctification. It is one of the great words of the Christian faith, and one of the most practical, because it answers a question every honest believer eventually asks: if I’m forgiven, why am I still like this — and does God intend to do anything about it?

The answer is yes, emphatically. Here is what sanctification is, who does the work, and how you can cooperate with what God is already doing in you.

The word, and what it means

To sanctify means to set apart, to make holy. At conversion, God declares a sinner righteous in Christ — that is justification, a verdict passed once and for all. Sanctification is what follows: the lifelong process by which God actually makes that person, in character and conduct, what he has already declared them to be. Justification changes your standing in a moment; sanctification changes your life over time. One is a courtroom, where the verdict is announced; the other is a workshop, where the announced reality is slowly, patiently worked into the grain of a life. Both are wholly the gift of God in Christ, and the two must never be separated: we are not made holy in order to be accepted, but because we already have been.

And it is not optional. God’s intention for every believer is spelled out plainly: “this is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4:3). The goal is nothing less than a restored likeness to Christ, and Scripture is sober about how much it matters: “Strive … for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord” (Hebrews 12:14). Sanctification is not a spiritual luxury for the keen; it is the ordinary shape of a real Christian life.

Whose work is it?

Here is where many go wrong in one of two directions. Some treat sanctification as entirely God’s work and their own effort as irrelevant — and drift. Others treat it as entirely their own project of self-improvement — and either despair or grow proud. Scripture holds both together in a single, striking sentence: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13).

Notice the order. We work because God works. Our effort is real — “work out” — but it is not the engine; it is the response to a deeper working that is God’s. He is the one who changes us: “we all … beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). The transformation is God’s doing, by his Spirit, as we behold Christ. Our part is to keep looking, and to stop resisting.

Holiness is a Person before it is a performance

Andrew Murray, in Holy in Christ, made a point easy to miss: our holiness is not first a set of behaviors we produce but a Person we are joined to. God’s people are called “saints” — literally “holy ones” — not because they have arrived but because they are set apart in Christ, who is himself their holiness. Sanctification, then, is not manufacturing holiness out of our own resources; it is letting the holiness of Christ, in whom we already stand, work its way out into how we actually live. Murray’s counsel was to stop striving to become holy in the flesh and instead to abide in the Holy One and let his life sanctify us from within.

This is why sanctification and joy are not enemies. Hannah Whitall Smith called her classic on the subject The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life, because she had discovered that the path to holiness is also the path to rest — a full surrender to God that hands him the whole self and trusts him to do the changing. Holiness pursued as grim self-effort exhausts; holiness received as the fruit of trust and surrender sets a person free.

This reframes the whole pursuit. The daily question of sanctification is not merely “am I trying hard enough to be good?” but “am I close enough to the Holy One to catch his life?” Effort that flows from union with Christ bears fruit; effort that substitutes for it only produces weariness or self-righteousness — the two ditches on either side of the road. A branch grows grapes not by straining but by staying joined to the vine; and a Christian grows holy not by gritted willpower alone but by staying joined to Christ and letting his holiness do its patient work. The effort is real, but it is the effort of a branch drawing sap, not a factory manufacturing fruit from nothing.

How it actually happens

So what does cooperation with God look like in practice? Scripture and the holiness writers point to a handful of ordinary means, none glamorous, all effective over time:

  • Reckon yourself dead to sin. Paul’s command is to count as true what Christ has made true: “consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus … do not let sin reign in your mortal body” (Romans 6:11–12). Sanctification begins by believing you are no longer sin’s slave, and living from that.
  • Walk by the Spirit. “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16). Holiness is less about white-knuckling against sin and more about yielding, moment by moment, to the Spirit who produces the fruit of Christ’s character in us.
  • Feed on the truth. Jesus prayed, “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth” (John 17:17). The mind soaked in Scripture is the mind God reshapes; there is no sanctification apart from his word.
  • Surrender, and keep surrendering. The decisive turn, Smith and Murray agreed, is the handing over of the whole self to God — not once, but as a settled posture. What is fully yielded, God is free to make holy.

Why am I still struggling with sin?

Here is the question that troubles honest believers most: if I am being sanctified, why do I still fail so often — sometimes in the very areas I have prayed hardest about? It helps enormously to know that this struggle is not a sign that something has gone wrong. It is the normal experience of a Christian in whom two powers are at war. Paul, no beginner, described it without embarrassment: “I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing” (Romans 7:19). The presence of the fight is not evidence of a false faith; the fight itself is evidence of new life, for the dead do not struggle against sin at all.

Scripture names the two combatants: “the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do” (Galatians 5:17). The Spirit has moved in, and the old flesh has not yet been evicted, and they contend. So do not read your ongoing struggle as failure and give up; read it as the war a living branch wages that a dead one never could. The direction matters more than the perfection: a sanctifying Christian is not one who never falls, but one who, by grace, is learning to fall less, grieve more quickly, and get up facing the same way. Discouragement is one of sin’s cleverest weapons; answer it not with excuses but with the cross, and get back in the fight.

A lifelong work, and a certain one

Sanctification is slow, and it is not linear. There are advances and painful setbacks; the closer we come to the light, the more we see what still needs cleansing. John Wesley pressed believers, in A Plain Account of Christian Perfection, to expect more of God’s transforming grace than they often dared — to believe that love could so fill a heart as to crowd out sin’s reign; and whatever one makes of his highest claims, his refusal to settle for a stagnant Christianity is bracing. God really does intend to change us, and deeply.

The great comfort is that the outcome is not in doubt. The God who began this work has bound himself to finish it: he “will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6), when he “will sanctify you completely” (1 Thessalonians 5:23) and we shall at last be like him. Your slow progress is not evidence that God has given up; it is evidence that he is still at work, and he does not abandon what he has begun. Keep beholding Christ, keep surrendering, keep walking in the Spirit — and trust the Workman to complete what only he can.
